claims.text: Adding approximately 1 at.% Al to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The improvement from Al addition will result from formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale.
A continuous alumina scale will slow oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta is a refractory high-entropy alloy containing no aluminum.
Equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta has a single-phase BCC microstructure and retains substantial strength at 900°C.
Conventional Al-free refractory high-entropy alloys such as Ti-V-Nb-Ta typically form an unprotective oxide scale at high temperature.
Approximately 1 at.% Al can be incorporated into the base refractory high-entropy alloy as the proposed intervention.
The beneficial oxidation-resistance effect should occur during 700–900°C exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere for durations such as 100 hours.
During high-temperature exposure, added Al will preferentially migrate to the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched Al will oxidize to form a uniform, slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 layer.
The alumina layer will reduce oxygen penetration, internal oxidation, and degradation relative to the undoped alloy.
The Al-doped alloy will exhibit at least 30% lower oxidation weight gain than the undoped alloy under identical conditions.
The Al-doped alloy will form a thinner and more protective oxide scale than the undoped alloy.
The beneficial effect is limited to an Al concentration window around 1 at.%.
Higher Al contents might cause brittle intermetallics or other deleterious phases.
Brittle intermetallic phases such as Laves phases generally reduce the ductility of refractory high-entropy alloys.
A protective alumina scale is expected to form only at temperatures of at least 700°C in oxidizing environments, with little effect at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres.
The proposed alumina-forming mechanism is well established in other high-temperature alloys.
The optimal Al concentration and its effects on ductility and phase stability in refractory high-entropy alloys remain experimentally undetermined.
